utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. At the close of play yesterday, Mr. Mansfield urged that if possible we might deliver our reasons on the application which was decided on Monday. I'm pleased to be able to say, Mr. Mansfield, we've managed to get some thoughts together in between other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The -- it's of course a decision in respect of the application of the Prosecution to cross-examine the present witness. For reasons which are obvious, the submissions were dealt with in private session and for that same reason I propose to deliver the decision in private session. If we could go there now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, good afternoon. If I could remind you of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Whiting: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buja. Are you able to hear me clearly and understand me?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of the session yesterday I asked you some questions and you gave me some answers on the topic of Klecka's role in organising units to go to the assistance of other units during fighting, this during the period of June and July of 1998. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention now please to the transcript of the interview with the OTP. It's page 47 of the Albanian transcript and page 43 of the English.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the page in Albanian, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's page 47, and it's about halfway down the page. And if we could switch to the Sanction, please, on the monitors. And, sir, I'd like to just have you watch --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "O.L.: All these fights in areas, the soldiers were fighting and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. overlapping each other? "S.B.: That's correct. "O.L.: When things like this were needed to do, was it the headquarters in Klecka that organised it or where did the orders come from? "S.B.: Yeah, Klecka. "O.L.: Okay. And how was -- how were you communicating during this time? "S.B.: By messengers. "O.L.: Okay. You had no phone or telephone? "S.B.: So there was a scarcity of means of communication, so two or three radios at most for the whole region of Lapusnik. "O.L.: Did commander Celiku appear at different points, during fighting for example? "S.B.: Yes, what I've seen -- yes, I've seen him being present during the fighting in Carraleve. That I was myself there or during the fighting in Fushtice. So he's been in the front lines, so to say. He's been when the fighting was going on. "O.L.: On the other hand, between the fightings did he visit the points? For example, did he come to Kroimire to see you? "S.B.: Yes. "O.L.: Okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Buja, when units had -- during this period that we're talking about, June and July of 1998, when there was fighting and units had to go to the assistance of other units, that was organised by Klecka. Right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Klecka has got a different meaning from what is here. I already explained that the period June/July is a long period. I have explained that there was Jakup Krasniqi there. I want to explain further that I met also other members of the General Staff, since I was a commander of the subzone. So here I'm talking about a rather lengthy period of time, June/July. I know that we have coordinated the actions among the units. Yesterday I said that one unit went to assist another unit when there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who from Klecka would organise units going to the assistance of other units during this time period, June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated yesterday that when in some fighting I needed assistance, I asked for it or other units came without inviting them. But when I saw that the situation was very hard -- difficult, then I asked other units to help and they did come. But when I talk about assistance, it's not what is being claimed in the sense of organising the fight through the organisation of the units. When there was fighting, the unit -- part of the unit of Klecka came to assist us because not all the unit could come. I think I already mentioned that Ymer Alushani or Voglushi, their units came or the Luzhnice unit and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the interview the question was: "When it was necessary to send a unit to the assistance of another unit, who organised that?" And you answered -- you said: "Klecka." So my question is: Who in Klecka organised that? Who did that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even at the time of the interview I thought that in Klecka there was a member of the General Staff. My brother was there, too, as a member of the General Staff. He was an advisor to the staff. Likewise, in Klecka in July other members of the General Staff came whom I got to know in July. In given periods of time in Klecka there was a kind of command, a sort of command. In June there was Jakup Krasniqi. Then of course he was replaced by someone else. Other members of the General Staff came there and they contacted also with Jakup Krasniqi. So this is what I'm talking about, this form of organisation. I saw Klecka always as the centre of visits or contacts that the General Staff kept with others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the other members of the General Staff that were in Klecka in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July they didn't stay there. I saw that other members came to Klecka like Hashim Thaqi; he even visited me to Blinaje. Then there was Sokol Bashota, Azem Syla. So they were members that stayed there one night, two nights, and then they went to other villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998, did Jakup Krasniqi ever organise units going to the assistance of other units during fighting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, he didn't -- he was not engaged in organisation, but it was through this person, through Jakup Krasniqi, that we received the necessary information, instructions from the General Staff as to how we should operate. He -- in a way he was a kind of liaison between the General Staff and us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this role as a liaison, did he transmit orders or instructions concerning units going to the assistance of other units during fighting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He transmitted information from the General Staff. He gave interviews. He gave -- he made communiques and he also relayed instructions. I already explained that it was from Jakup Krasniqi that I received the nomination, my nomination, as a commander of the subzone issued by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, please listen to my questions carefully. The instructions that he relayed, did they concern -- did they ever concern during June and July of 1998 organising units going to the assistance of other units during fighting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have to repeat what I already stated, that Jakup Krasniqi passed to us, that is transmitted to us, the instructions of the General Staff also regarding the organisation of the units, the form of this organisation. I am saying and repeating that they were organising units which was a horizontal form of organisation. And the assistance we gave to each other or to one unit or another, as I say, was like this, one unit went to assist another unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, you say that you're repeating yourself, but I submit to you that you have not answered the question. The question is: Did these instructions that were -- that you say were transmitted by the General Staff through Jakup Krasniqi, did they ever relate to units going to the assistance of other units during fighting? If you could please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to answer the question. I'm saying you that I believe I have explained it, namely that in June I contacted Jakup Krasniqi. He gave me instructions on the form of organisation of the subzones, and I began the coordination of the units which I mentioned earlier; that is, Jakup Krasniqi gave me instructions on the organisation of the unit, the coordination of this unit, which was something normal to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those -- please focus on assistance during fighting. Did those instructions on the organisation of the units include organising -- units assisting other units during fighting? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering the questions continuously. I'm saying that the assistance given from one unit to another was part of the strategy of the General Staff, because we couldn't help assisting a unit when that unit needed us. It was a normal thing to do. The form of organisation, as I said, was from one unit to another, and the coordination of actions among all the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've now said that the assistance given from one unit to another unit was part of the strategy of the General Staff. And that's a partial answer, I would submit. But the question is in specific instances, when there was fighting in an area and another unit had to come assist that unit during fighting, would instructions be transmitted by the General Staff -- by the General Staff through Jakup Krasniqi? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question; it was rather long. I couldn't concentrate on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat the question. The question is: You have now said that "the assistance given from one unit to another unit was part of the strategy of the General Staff." The question is: In specific instances when there was fighting in an area and another unit had to come to assist that unit during fighting, would instructions be transmitted by the General Staff through Jakup Krasniqi? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say with yes or no. Anyway, my question -- my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll put to the same question with respect to the other members of the General Staff that you identified spent time in Klecka, Sokol Bashota and Azem Syla. Did either of them ever transmit instructions -- give instructions regarding one unit assisting another unit during fighting? And if you could answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the period. I said I met them in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's focus on the area of June and July of 1998. In the area of Klecka, when they were in Klecka, did they -- either one of them ever give instructions regarding one unit assisting another unit during fighting, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot answer with a yes or no. I already said that in June I did not meet them; it was in July when I met them. And in July of course we received information, instructions, because I was the subzone commander. I was introduced to them as member -- they were introduced to me as members of the General Staff. But I cannot say yes or no for a two-month period which was rife in events, dramatic events, events that developed very fast. So I couldn't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember things in July because at that time we contacted the General Staff members, other members who introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in July did any General Staff member in Klecka organise one unit assisting another unit during fighting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I know that the General Staff members gave instructions at certain moments. When there was fighting somewhere, the instruction was given for the unit to go to another unit when there was fierce fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that ever occur from Klecka? Were those instructions ever given from Klecka?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, instructions came also from Klecka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen during June or July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened especially in July when there was very savage offensive and we tried to coordinate as best as we could affairs with the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact those instructions came from Fatmir Limaj in Klecka, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions from Fatmir Limaj in the sense of hierarchy, they were not; but during contacts, especially at the end of June and the beginning of July, we discussed the possibility of coordinating the actions of the unit. But instructions per se, in the hierarchic sense, didn't come from Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically who they came from if they didn't come from Fatmir Limaj? You've said that "the instructions came from Klecka, that they came in July of 1998." My question is: Who gave the instructions, if not Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received instructions and clarification or notifications, orders, in July from the General Staff through Jakup Krasniqi. I said there were also other members of the General Staff and -- whom I contacted in July and through whom I got instructions or other notifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but you told us that Jakup Krasniqi never transmitted orders or instructions relating to units assisting other units. So the question is: Who -- if it's -- not Jakup Krasniqi, if not Fatmir Limaj, who from Klecka during July of 1998 transmitted instructions about units assisting other units?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I knew the members of the General Staff who were dealing with the organisation of this form of warfare. I knew Azem Syla, who much later I knew as general commander. I knew Sokol Bashota also as a member of the General Staff, who also was engaged in the organisation. And normally I received instructions from them. This was one form of organisation at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of instructions did you receive from them at that time, could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July I received instructions, orders, orders which applied to the Nerodime subzone, orders or -- on -- or the form of restructuring of the units, the organisation of the command of the subzone, the functioning of the units. That is, I received these circulars, orders, from the General Staff in my capacity as commander of a subzone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about in July during what you described as the very savage offensive? Were either Sokol Bashota or Azem Syla involved in coordinating the units during that fighting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were, because the offensive was very wide and they moved in the territory of Malisheve municipality. There was -- at that time the General Staff was active in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they did that at the end of July during the offensive, were either one of them in Klecka?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in July at different periods. There were frequent visits by the General Staff members in Klecke, but I also met them in other villages, especially with Sokol Bashota I met in Malisheve when we had to send soldiers from my subzone to get armed supplies in Albania. I contacted very often with the members of the General Staff then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was more specific. At the end of July during the offensive when you say that these -- that Sokol Bashota and Azem Syla were involved in coordinating the units, were either one of them in Klecka when they were doing this?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they stayed for certain periods, two, three days in Klecke, and for some other days in other villages, like Javor, Terpeze villages, villages which were close to Klecke; or in Malisheve for two, three days. I could contact these people and more often I contacted them in Klecke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your answer, but if you could answer this question: Do you know if either one of them was in Klecka during the first offensive at the end of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they have -- they stayed in Klecke for certain periods of time and that in July I met them very often. I couldn't tell you whether they were in Klecke each and every day, but I did contact them in Klecke, in Javor, and in Terpeze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could go back to what you said in the interview, please, when it was asked -- when the question was asked: "Which was the commanding unit or centre that organised assistance going from one unit to another unit?" And you said: "Klecka." Is it your testimony now that you were referring to what you've just testified about, the first offensive?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the first offensive, I am referring to Klecka regarding contacts with the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- but you didn't say that in the interview, did you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have often stated that it is because of the mistakes that may have occurred during this interview and that often after the war I have called the place Klecke without making any explanation -- detailed explanations as to who was there and so on. So you have to understand that it is very difficult after such a long period of time for someone to recollect events and especially with such accuracy that you demand here. I'm trying to say what I remember as it was then. And this is the truth that I'm repeating every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, later in the -- later in this passage you say that: "At this time communication was by courier," and that's right, that's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. true, isn't it, that you communicated with other units by courier?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By courier I meant a soldier. It was not a designated person as such. I just told the soldier, for example, to go from one unit to another if I needed that. It wasn't any, as I said, designated person as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I understand. And when you said there's no -- there was no radio or telephone at the time and you said there were no more than two or three radio links in the whole area of Lapusnik, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I could remember and even today I have this impression that radio links as far as I could remember were very few. Indeed where I was operated, I didn't know that there was any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you then say that during -- you're asked if during the fighting if Commander Celiku was present and you said that he came during the fighting at Carraleve and the fighting at Fustica. And that's true, isn't it, that happened? He came to the fighting in Carraleve and Fustica. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for July, I know that Commander Celiku came to Kroimire. He came to fightings. As well as for June I don't remember such a thing. I mentioned it yesterday, that Fatmir mentioned me -- Fatmir visited me in Kroimire and in Blinaje. We were comrades in arms and we were in a closer relationship with each other than we had with others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on this passage when "he would come also when there wasn't fighting," and that's also true, you've told us that, he would come to the units, for example, in Kroimire when there wasn't fighting. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that in Kroimire there was no unit, but he came to visit me. I was staying there, sleeping there. We went together to Blinaje where we visited Blinaje in the capacity of a national treasure because it was a place rich in flora and fauna. The visits with Fatmir were very frequent in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I'm going to move to a different topic and that is the topic of Lapusnik. During June and July of 1998, did you ever go to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot precise the exact time. As for June/July, I visited Lapusnik region. For me it was difficult to know Lapusnik village where the houses of this village were. As a region, I knew it as a mountainous region. It has scattered houses and it is difficult to determine which exact place is Lapusnik and from where to where it extends. Even today I don't know exactly where the borders of Lapusnik village lie. I was there during June/July in the region of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you go during June and July to the region of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I were -- I was there twice, although my going to this region could have happened on another occasion in addition to these two, but it is possible that I didn't know whether I was in Lapusnik or somewhere else. I could have as well been in Negroc or in the territory of Kishna Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without -- I don't want you to give -- use a name in response to this question, but did you go -- was there an occasion where you went to Lapusnik for a particular reason related to a particular person?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went for a designated person in the region of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, could you tell us why it is you went to the Lapusnik region with respect to this person. What caused you to go?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What caused me to go was the visit that his father paid me and his story that his son was taken by the soldiers of the KLA. He didn't know the reasons, but he knew that the person who took his son, according to him, was Voglushi, a soldier at Lapusnik. And myself, since I knew Voglushi, I set off in order to meet him and explain this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when this person's father told you this story?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning I wasn't there, but I met him when I came back from a place which I don't remember now. I probably was there with some unit. So I met him when I arrived in Kroimire, where I was stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then travel from Kroimire to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I travelled to the region of Lapusnik to the positions or to the places manned by soldiers of the KLA along that front line. I thought I could find Voglushi in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the positions or places manned by the soldiers of the KLA along the front line, that's in Lapusnik, isn't it, Lapusnik village?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Lapusnik as part of the place where the warfare was waged comprises of a lengthy front line and certain units or their scattering in the houses was quite wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you go precisely?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I went to the village of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got there, who did you see?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived I first met with soldiers who escorted me to Voglushi, who was staying in a house in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that trip did you also see Isak Musliu, Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Isak Musliu in that region and there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that same trip?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, I think yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, what happened when -- what happened next when you went to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contacted a person who I knew and with whom I had contacts even before, that is Voglushi, and I asked him as for this person where he was if he was there. Voglushi of course explained to me that that person was there and that he was stopped by him due to some violations that he had committed and some addresses that were found in his vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what the violations were?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he told me because we were in good terms with him. He told me that this person was driving very fast and put the life of the civilians there at risk. He did not respect the stop sign by the soldiers, so he was forced to stop. When his vehicle was checked, certain addresses of Serbs were found and Voglushi thought that these addresses could be of Serb inspectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get -- did he give you any other reason that he had been stopped and brought to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any other reasons except for his fast driving and his refusal to stop. He was stopped to be verified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long before you went to Lapusnik he had been -- he had been stopped?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't be able to remember this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you tell Voglushi, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that I knew this person's family and I knew that this family had no suspicion -- it was not suspected of its activities. And of course I guaranteed for him by saying that I knew his family and his father, and I told him that his actions should not be suspected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you "knew his family had no suspicion or should not be suspected of its activities," what exactly were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely about those addresses, Serb names, that they had found, those that Voglushi suspected were addresses of Serb inspectors. Of course I said that it was a good family and that there was no way that they had any connections with Serb inspectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you arrived, do you know if anybody had done any investigation of this person after he was stopped?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for questioning, investigation, I don't know. I don't know to this date. But I know he was stopped for the reasons that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you met with Voglushi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a region of Lapusnik. I thought I was in Lapusnik, but I don't remember the period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I meant -- I meant were you in a house? Were you outside? What kind of a building, if any?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection it was a village house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was present when you met with Voglushi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many soldiers during that meeting with Voglushi because soldiers were staying there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Qerqiz present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a visit that I paid to Voglushi; it wasn't a scheduled meeting, a special meeting. I just went there. And to my recollection, Qerqiz was amongst them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Fatmir Limaj amongst them there during that visit to Voglushi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think your answer was heard. You have to speak up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you gave this information to Voglushi?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voglushi called this person, and this person came. I saw him with his hands untied, his hands were not tied. I even asked him if -- in case he was maltreated. He said, No, at least he said no, and I did not notice any changes on his appearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, I took this person with me and we wanted to set off for Kroimire. We tried to give him his vehicle back, the vehicle that he had, but he didn't want to accept this although we insisted, both myself and Voglushi, we insisted that he took his car. But he swore and -- in the name of his children, saying that he wanted to leave his vehicle to the service of the KLA, which he called his army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what happened? How did you leave that place?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I walked back to Kroimire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how he left?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we left that place together but I'm not quite sure because it's difficult for me to remember all these moments from the war, but I believe that we left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will assume at just after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, during June and July of 1998, did you hear of other instances of Albanians being arrested or detained because they were suspected of being collaborators?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit, for your information, had its own place of detention. We had asked them to give us their bio data and when they were not from the region where we were stationed we asked them why they were there, to give us the reasons why they were there. So this happened in June/July of that year.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Stopping place," probably he meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Were there other instances of Albanians being arrested or detained because they were suspected of being collaborators?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases of collaborators, I have not heard; but as I have explained earlier, we have stopped people because I myself have stopped some people and asked them, as I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on the circumstances when you would stop people?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Often soldiers, myself, have stopped someone who wanted to penetrate a territory controlled by the KLA. We asked him to show us his ID and also asked him why he had been to that place where he wanted to go. I can give you many examples, but another example that I remember very well is that of my brother. He also went to that territory and soldiers stopped him and they detained him for some time, one or two hours I think. And after my arrival there, I too started to suspect what he was saying, namely that he wanted to meet Jakup Krasniqi in Negrovce. I was suspicious of how my brother, my own brother, could know where Jakup Krasniqi was, where I personally didn't know that he was in Negrovce. My brother lived and worked in Pristina and for me it didn't make sense that he knew about Jakup Krasniqi's whereabouts. After my brother insisted that he didn't know that Jakup Krasniqi was in Negrovce but that he was born in that place and probably he could find some information from his family as to his whereabouts now, that is then. So in that circumstance, I accompanied my brother with a soldier in the direction of Klecke so that he could penetrate in Negrovce, where he wanted to go. There have been other cases with doctors in July who we prevented -- we delayed from going to treat soldiers wounded in the fighting in Rahovec and in other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you delay those doctors, for what reason? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those doctors told us that they were doctors, we would have of course have tried to find that out or to find out whether they harboured another intention in trying to go to that place. So keeping them there, stopping them from one or two hours in Blinaje once, the General Staff criticised us for doing that because we had delayed them. But if we didn't know people, who they were, we stopped them, did not allow them to go into the war territory. So it was only when they insisted very much then we could think twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's put aside cases where people were stopped or delayed simply because they were unknown. Were there instances where Serbs were stopped or arrested?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I once detained -- stopped a car in Carraleve where -- when I saw a young Serb boy who was stopped by the soldiers there. Since the soldiers saw him to be a Serb, they thought that maybe he was one of the security or the military or the police. He was a very young boy and I told them, It can't be that he's a member of any of these forces, so they released him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the soldiers who stopped this young boy?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the name of the soldiers who stopped that boy, but I do know that he was stopped by the soldiers in Carraleve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in collecting weapons from people, from their houses or from their persons?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the war period. Either the civilians who possessed weapons came and surrendered those weapons to the KLA or there were other cases when people were in legal possession of arms given to them by the occupiers. So in those cases we intervened and made sure that these weapons could be used by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to a house to collect weapons?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to get a weapon of someone who had -- in Magura it was, someone who had a weapon with permission and that place was close to the positions of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you went there?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to that house. It was night. We couldn't move during the day in territories where the occupiers where. We went there. We knocked on the door and the owner of the house appeared. And then we asked him is that he has information about a weapon given to him by permission of the occupiers, and then he handed us over the weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other instances where you went to a house to collect weapons?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other instances that I recall were after my return to Kosova, when I came subzone commander. When I went to Katim [phoen] village and got some weapons there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other instances aside from the case that you described of the young boy who was stopped of Serbs being arrested or detained because they were suspected of being either police or military?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say he was arrested. He was stopped at that stopping place that we had, and that after my arrival there and after my comment on his young age and my words to the soldiers that he couldn't be a member of the violent forces of Serbia, then he was allowed to continue on his way. So it wasn't an arrest. It was a stop at this checkpoint, let's say, and then I remember another case of a car, emergency car, that I myself stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also in Carraleve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you stopped him?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information that the Serb occupiers were moving by ambulance cars and in disguise they moved about. That's why I went to Carraleve pass to observe and see whether Serb forces were moving by such cars, and I stopped one such and ordered it to go in the direction of Kroimire where I thought to send it. And he -- the driver came and followed me up to Kroimire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you got in Kroimire?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got to Kroimire -- when he came out of the car, I saw that he had become very scared. He was trembling and shaking. Probably this was the first time for him to see KLA soldiers. And he was speaking not in pure Albanian, even though he was trying hard to speak Albanian. But later on I realised that he was a Goran or Turk, of Turk nationality. And in my talk with him I told him not to worry, that we are the army of Kosova and we don't want to deal with the civilian population of any nationality it may be, and he became calmer. On the next day, that night he stayed there. He stayed at the same place where I stayed as far as I remember. On the next day he left for Prizren. Before he left where his place of birth was, Prizren, I remember I gave him 100 marks, Deutschmarks, because he had a family, he had children, and he had no money to go back to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from these examples that you have given us, are you aware of other instances, whether you were involved or not, of Serbs being stopped or detained?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the instances that I recall, but I know that every unit had a place, a stopping place, where they asked people to show them their identification papers, respecting the rules of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- before the break you talked about an example of a person who was stopped you said for driving too fast, dangerously, and then addresses of Serb inspectors were found in the person's car and he was detained on suspicion of having a -- some improper relationship with those Serb inspectors. Are you aware of other instances during June and July of 1998 when Albanians were stopped or detained for similar suspicions?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either misinterpreted to me or mistranslated or misinterpreted by you. I didn't say that they found addresses -- addresses of Serb inspectors, but there were suspicions that those Serb addresses might be addresses of Serb inspectors. But as to other cases, at least now I don't seem to recollect any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- during June and July of 1998 when individuals were stopped or detained in areas where you were, did you ever send those people to Klecka?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During July especially, the Blinaje unit had taken firm orders not to allow any civilians to penetrate into that national complex which was a national asset. So people's insistence to go into that place was not granted to them, only in very special cases, as the case was with my own brother. Then we accompanied them with soldiers in the direction of Klecka. In July Klecka became the passing -- a place where many people went. A new road was opened from Shale that led to Klecka or from Negrovce to Klecka, to people could go in the direction of Malisheve. Even when we didn't want to allow people to go further, I didn't feel I had the power or the competence to prevent people from going further because they insisted on going to Malisheve. There were many of them. Because in Malisheve there was a marketplace for the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you would accompany people with soldiers in the direction of Klecka in July, when was that in July?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my appointment as subzone commander, the soldiers were allowed to go -- to send people -- to allow people to go to Klecka. We didn't want to create problems, especially after the concentration of the Serb forces in the region I was operating. This was the period of July when we acted in this form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those people that you accompanied to Klecka, were those people under arrest?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not arrested but they were escorted by soldiers because normally we showed them the way where -- how -- the way which they followed to go where they wanted. But we also saw it as -- as an extra responsibility on our part to take care and see where the people were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn to page 69 of the Albanian transcript, page 60 of the English transcript. And on the Albanian on page 69, it's about halfway through the page, and on the English it's also halfway through the page. And if -- okay, I see we have the Sanction up on the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt. Before Mr. Whiting embarks on that, what has been happening prior to this when passages from this interview have been put, Mr. Whiting has been about to cross-examine the witness. I have to say, and I may be the only one in the room to say it, but in reading and listening carefully to your ruling, I did not understand that to be a remit for cross-examination in relation to matters raised in evidence beyond the point when the application was made. If I have misunderstood the situation, then I'll be corrected, of course. But if that's what is about to happen, may I raise, therefore, the prospect, if I am right, that this would require another application, and the foundation laid therefor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not been my experience I must confess, Mr. Topolski. A witness having been declared is then dealt with throughout the balance of the evidence on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Nor am I, particularly when a witness -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- I think I'm saying the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You're saying the opposite?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, then I am alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't feel concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, no, it's sometimes the best place to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a matter of interest and significant to raise, but without either of us going into detail at the moment, for obvious reasons, I would not be minded to interrupt what is now happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the clip could be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "O.L.: Were you -- can you tell us if you were involved in arresting people that were considered Serb collaborators. "S.B.: No, I haven't been involved directly in these sort of operations or actions. So I've been involved in the weapons collections, meaning from people who we knew that had weapons. There is a case in Magura. We collected a rifle and a revolver. Also gorge of Carraleve is another case. So I took a vehicle and the driver of that vehicle, he was emergency aid vehicle. So he was frightened because he thought he was being arrested because on the same day he was released because the target of this action was not the person but the vehicle. Or another case is that when I took a 17-years-old boy. He was a Serb. He of course was released later. He serves actually as a police in Lipjan. But as far as the arrest cases are concerned, yeah, there have been cases where arrests are made. And the most difficult period was this period, June/July. There have been cases that -- which I cannot name by first name and family name because I don't know. But I can say also that there's a sort of personal revenge, settling scores for personal motives because there was enough -- there were sufficient conditions or enough spite to engage in such acts. Because of these -- these scattered units operating in all the area. But I am -- refused, I haven't accepted to set up or assign a place as a place to detain or to arrest people because I -- I didn't think of myself as competent for this job. And I didn't even consider myself as a man who had such -- so much knowledge as to do so this. And if -- when arrests took place and when I'm asked what to do, well, I just would instruct the person who would approach and ask me these questions, this case -- these case, bring him to Klecka or send him to Klecka. Because as I said, I wasn't the person with well-defined responsibilities. "O.L.: Yes. I'm sorry. We have to interrupt just for a minute. I'll change the tape because the tape is at an end."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I want to ask you about a few things that you said in that passage that we've just played. You said that "cases of arrests did happen and indeed the most serious time was precisely June and July." And that's true, isn't it, that cases of arrests happened and the most serious time was June and July?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this statement I mentioned the taking of this person with his vehicle, but it wasn't an arrest. And other cases that could have happened and were called arrests, because that's how I referred to them according to the interpretation made by people about those who were stopped at that time. Therefore, I did not exclude the possibility due to the extension of the guerrilla units, the possibility of individual revenge. I did not mention a particular case of individual revenge, but there were such as hearsay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you about cases of personal revenge in a moment, but it's true, isn't it, that the most serious time of arrests was in June and July of 1998, as you said in the interview? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time is the most difficult as per the words spoken in relation to arrests. I did not know such -- of such an arrest, but this was the most difficult time to -- when it was spoken of these arrests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you then mention and you've already referred to it in your -- in response to my previous question, but you mention in the interview that there were cases -- there was also personal revenge and that there was plenty of scope for acts of this kind. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this I wanted to stress that people were armed and in addition there were places where people whom -- with whom we coordinated later not to get out of control of the KLA. There were people who had special reasons of their -- for their actions, to compromise us. And due to the extension, wide extension of the guerrilla units, there was space for individual acts that could have happened. Simply, the guerrilla units extended in a wide area and be coming out of the people and the units that were still not under our control could leave space for such acts [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of instances -- any instances where in areas under KLA control people were detained or arrested as the result of personal revenge?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not specify a case familiar to me, but there were words about the Dukagjini area, where entire villages and villagers were armed on their own initiative because this was an area close to Albania and these villages could not be controlled by the KLA into the structures of this army. In this -- such cases could have happened even in the territory where we operated and it was difficult for us to control all the cases. I cannot speak of a concrete case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to focus, please, on areas where the KLA was in control. In those areas did you ever hear of instances where people were arrested or detained as a result of personal revenge?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were cases, but I do not remember a specific one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember hearing about any cases like that in the areas around Klecka in the villages of Kroimire, Luznica, Lapusnik, Blinaje, any of those areas during June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially in July during the offensive there was gossip about these events interpreted in different ways, but I do not know of any particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate at all on what this gossip, as you describe it, was? What did you hear during July?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During July, as I explained, a special war was waged against the KLA and this war incorporated these rumours as well as per different acts perpetrated by KLA members, that people were being taken, people were being arrested. I would like to explain here that people who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stopped in order not to go directly to the hands of the enemy, this stopping was interpreted by the population in a wrong way and the population would react in that way by saying that they were arrested. In other words, even if we have good intentions not to allow people to penetrate into territories where they could have been killed, in this context arrest was interpreted wrongly. There were cases when both myself and Jakup Krasniqi, we were said to have -- these were words that were circulating at this time when allegedly we had a person with 2.000 Deutschmarks in Switzerland, and we never actually have this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of the passage of the interview that I played for you you said, "When I happened to be at an arrest and when I was asked what, what should I do, I simply said: Send him to Klecka, meaning in fact send him to Klecka because I did not know of anywhere else." And that's in fact what you did, isn't it, Mr. Buja, during June and July of 1998? When persons were arrested in your area, you gave instructions to send them to Klecka.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it is spoken of arrest here, it refers to the escort of the person that we suspected had entered the war territory with special intentions. Simply, this was about the isolation of that person so that he could not harm our positions. We would then escort this person, assign two, three soldiers to escort them to Klecka, and we controlled the journey to the destination. This was kind of a security measure in order to secure our position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when this happened, when persons you suspected entered the war territory with special intentions, are you talking about Serbs or Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to Albanians because Serbs did not enter that territory. Serbs rarely entered that territory, only when they would use the road Peja-Pristina. The Albanians who were suspect of being collaborators were known to the entire population and they did not enter this territory. The territories that were controlled by the KLA were usually penetrated by different persons who we didn't know and whose intentions were not familiar with us, therefore we had to be cautious in our actions. I will here illustrate this issue with another example. If the person did not tell us the reason of his visit and insisted on going to his destination, as is the case with Adem Demaqi, a well-known personality, we would then keep that person for five hours in a row until he told us the reason of his journey and then we would escort him to the area of Klecka. I am not the person who could assume responsibility for stopping those people were returning them back, but my responsibility was to pay attention for the territories where I was operating and the soldiers who I assigned to escort the persons in the direction of Klecka. In Klecka there was also -- there were also civilian population who could know the person that we stopped, and that's why we actually directed them in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn to page 73 of the transcript in Albanian; it's page 62 in English. On page 62 it's towards the top that we'll begin. On page 73 it's also at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could switch to the Sanction, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "A.C.: Your own sort of limited involvement in these events. Here I'm talking about the abductions. But you were aware that many individuals were being abducted, many Albanians and Serbs were being abducted at this time, even if you personally were not directly involved in abducting these people. So your answer is yes? Yeah, yeah. And you're aware of Serbs that were abducted as well? "S.B.: Yeah, I can talk about my case. I cannot talk -- I cannot talk about the abduction of Serb civilians other than the cases what I myself witnessed. "A.C.: But you heard about other Serbs that were abducted even if you were not yourself involved and present? "S.B.: Yes. There was -- there were rumours that there were people from the secret service and military personnel were being captured. But there is never mentioned a case of civilians. "A.C.: And you mentioned a moment ago that when an inquiry was made of you, you actually directed that the person go to Klecka? "S.B.: Yes. "A.C.: Was that a collection point in Klecka during this time period, during June and July of 1998, for people who had been arrested? "S.B.: I don't know whether they might -- they were to be taken, but I directed people there because I know they're people of higher authority. "A.C.: Because essentially Klecka was your superior sort of formation? "S.B.: Yeah, as a matter of fact I would get instructions from the Commander Celiku. "A.C.: Do you know any of the locations where people that were arrested were taken after they left Klecka? "S.B.: Well, there was -- I'm -- I know about the locations of there being -- there being gossiping around amongst the soldiers and even among civilian populations. "A.C.: And Lapusnik was one of those locations. Correct? "S.B.: Lapusnik was mentioned in the context of -- as a place of where people were being detained and then later released. I myself had -- I myself have escorted people on their way back home, people released -- "A.C.: People that were released from Lapusnik? "S.B.: Yes. People are being detained, interrogated, and then later released. "A.C.: So there was definitely a camp" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, did you see at the beginning of that clip that was played you were asked -- it was put to you that you were aware of the fact that many of the people, that is, Albanians and Serbs, were being kidnapped at this time and you nodded your head "yes" on the tape. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's true, you were aware that at this time during June and July 1998, many people, Albanians and Serbs, were being kidnapped. Right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I said that I heard about this. This is in a sense how I interpreted the words that I heard and I stated that I could only speak of cases that I attended, as were the cases that I described earlier. The interpretation of the people being stopped was in many cases as arrest. And this applies to the way I stopped the person from Prizren. I cannot say that there were kidnapping or arrested, I just described the words that were used by different people and by soldiers regarding these actions. I of course could not accept or even think that there was a camp or prison there. I simply thought at that time and I think today -- I'm convinced here that people were just stopped. They were identified. The reasons of them being there were found out and then people were released to proceed with their journey. It is something else how the questions were asked, but this is the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I understand that Mr. Whiting has asked a question with regard to the body language of the witness on the tape as opposed to the actual language used by the witness in the interview. I'm not clear as to whether or not or perhaps his interpretation of the language on the interview is somewhat distinct from mine, but it seemed as if he is at this point, if I'm not mistaken, attempting to use body language that he has seen on the tape to dispute the actual language that is contained in the statement. I'm not positive that's what he's doing, but I have that as a concern. I also have as a concern, there have been a number of questions now in which we have been dealing with gossip and rumours, and I understand that hearsay is admissible in these proceedings, but I would note for the record an objection with regard to the Trial Chamber's reliance on any gossip or rumours that have been elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I think you can be confident of that not occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see then, Mr. Buja, where you say that you sent -- you sent people who were arrested to Klecka because "I thought that the people most responsible for these matters were at Klecka." And then you're asked if that was because Klecka was a command post for you and you say in fact I received instructions there from Commander Celiku. That is in fact why you sent people who were arrested to Klecka, isn't it, because the people most responsible for those matters were in Klecka? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am telling you the truth for days now. Instruction is something else, an order something else. I received instructions from many others because in conversations with them of course I accepted those instructions that were good and those that were not for me to use I did not consider those instructions. This is not in a sense of order but in sense of cooperation with Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've anticipated by -- you've given an answer to a question that I haven't asked yet, but if we could go back to the question that I did ask which is: You sent people who were arrested to Klecka in this time period, June/July 1998, and -- the reason being you thought people most responsible for these matters, that is arrests, were in Klecka. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation of the word "arrest" here is wrong. I cannot say that I've arrested people. I stopped people. And when I was suspicious of them, I of course tried to clarify what was in question why that person was in that territory, and of course when I was not able to decide I sent them to Klecka in a sense that there there were people who could know them. There were also people from General Staff who could orient these people and say what to do with them, where to send them, whether they should be allowed to enter war territories or not. This is the sense of this action and not the arrest you are putting here because I believe that this interview I gave, in it I could not think that people could be imprisoned because I understood that prison should have investigation part and therefore I cannot interpret it as an arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those people in Klecka who could say what to do with them, where to send them, included Commander Celiku. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Klecke they knew of course to give people directions as to where to go. They could tell those people if they wanted to go to some village in Malisheve municipality or in Drenica or Dukagjin area. At that time, people could move through war territories --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you. My question is: The people in Klecka that you're referring to included Commander Celiku. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that were in Klecke, the soldiers, the population there could give instructions to these people as to what route they should follow or where to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, you have not answered my question and I just have to ask it again then. The people who were in Klecka included Commander Celiku. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were in Klecka of course comprised also -- included Commander Celiku, but in the sense that is used here I cannot say that Celiku or Fatmir Limaj was included. He was there with his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say then that Lapusnik was always "mentioned as being a place where people were detained, detained and released." And that's true, isn't it, during this time period, during June and July of 1998? Lapusnik was a place where people were detained and sometimes released?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked here specifically about Lapusnik. As to detention places or otherwise stopping places or checkpoints, I explained to you what I meant by that word. In this case I was asked about Lapusnik and I knew that there was such a place also in Lapusnik where people were stopped and they were asked to produce their identification papers. They were asked about the purpose of them being in the war territory. And of course when they had been released or allowed to go further with their journey, this detention or this stopping of the people might have lasted a couple of hours, one, two hours. That was the purpose of that process. This is how I see it in my description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware in June and July of 1998 of people being detained in Lapusnik for longer than one or two hours? For days?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact that people were stopped, as they were stopped in every checkpoint of our units. This is how I saw the meaning of the word "detained." As to how long they were -- they were detained, this I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, with respect to the case, the specific case that you told us about - and again without mentioning the name - which caused you to go to Lapusnik, how did you know that the person was in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say here that you escorted people who were released from Lapusnik. You've given us one example. Without mentioning names, were there other examples when you escorted people who were released from Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there have been other examples when either I myself or my soldiers have escorted people, when they have demanded that, when they wanted to go to other territories. The word "release" is used in the sense of being allowed to continue on their journey after being stopped for one hour or two or one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there instances when you escorted people being released from Lapusnik, aside from the one -- the specific example you've already given us?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the civilians who managed to enter into our territories were stopped and there has -- may have been some instance, which I don't recall now, of them being detained in Lapusnik and then being escorted further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you cannot recall any other specific examples at this time?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific examples, but I do know that during the offensive, especially on the 23rd and 24th of July, I stopped some tractors whose owners insisted on passing on to the territory controlled by the Serbs. And I was -- I told them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Could you ask him to repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not understand -- hear or understand the last part of your answer. You said you "stopped some tractors whose owners insisted on passing on to the territory controlled by the Serbs" and then you said something else.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you another question on this topic. At this time or shortly after, after the offensive at the end of July 1998 did you meet a group of men on a tractor who said that they were from Lapusnik, that they had been released from the Lapusnik prison?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I tried to explain earlier. This is the way the civilians interpreted the fact of us stopping them, in this case the tractors that wanted to go in the villages of the plain. This happened when we didn't want to allow them to go to Serb-controlled areas, and they have interpreted it as an arrest or a detention. On the 23rd and 24th in the morning I stopped -- of July, I stopped some tractors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a instance when you stopped a tractor with -- let me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. finish the question, please -- when you stopped a tractor with a group of men who said that they had been released or that they were from the Lapusnik prison?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I stopped tractors. I know that I stopped a tractor with some men, five or six men - I'm not very sure about the number - who interpreted it in their own way, something which I didn't like to hear. They told me that they were detained in Lapusnik. And the way I saw it was that they were prevented from going to other territories. If I'm not mistaken, this happened on the 23rd or the 24th of July; it was morning. Because in the evening there was fighting and I was taking part in the fighting. So I stopped the tractors -- we stopped the tractors because that was a rule. We didn't want to allow people to go in the direction of the plateau, in the direction of the Serb forces, because it was dangerous for them to enter that territory. I'm repeating here that it was difficult for us to stop those tractors, and we were in great dilemmas because this act was interpreted in various ways, even though our goal was not to allow them to go further because of the great danger facing them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I'm not focused on our act of stopping the tractor; I'm focused on who you saw on a tractor and I will -- and what they told you had happened to them. And you are putting it on the 23rd or the 24th. Did you stop another tractor on the 26th or 27th, a few days later, with a group of men who said that they had been in a prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of July I returned from the fighting in Jezerce where I was the commander of the subzone. On the 22nd and 23rd of July I went to search weapons, I heard they had weapons in the village of Dukagjin. There were armed villagers there. On the 22nd and 23rd I was on my way to and from that territory. On the 23rd and 24th of value, I was in Kroimire. On the 24th in the afternoon, as far as I remember, fighting broke out in Fushtice, where I participated -- I even participated in the operation to recapture the positions of the Fushtice unit --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, on the 26th and 27th of July, were you back in Kroimire?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to explain precisely that. From Fushtice I went to Blinaje area where fighting was going on. And on the 25th and 26th I was in the fighting that occurred in Zborce; it was a combined operation, Blinaje and Zborce units. I sent a soldier to inform the unit, on the 26th I think it was, the unit in Carraleve to withdraw. And until 2.00 p.m. of the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, Mr. Buja, I appreciate the detail, but you're giving a long answer to a very simple question. On the 26th or 27th were you in Kroimire?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was in Kroimire on the 26th and 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about one tractor that you stopped with people who said that they were -- had been detained in Lapusnik. Was that the only tractor you stopped with people who said they were detained in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tractors that we stopped in Lapusnik - there were others, of course - there were civilians, women, children on them. And they wanted to go to the villages of the plain. It was the beginning of the fierce offensive of 23rd and 24th of July. I may have stopped some other tractors, but not in Kroimire, in Shale or somewhere else. After the 27th when I felt I was in a better situation than before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there one tractor where the men said they were -- they had been detained in Lapusnik or did that happen more than once or was it just once?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tractor with only men as far as I remember. There was a tractor I remember I stopped in Kroimire. It was on the 23rd or the 24th of July. There were four -- five, six men at the most in that tractor and I stopped them in order to prevent them from going to the place they wanted to go, to the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you stopped them -- first of all, did they tell you that they had been in a prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that they had been detained in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that happened, did you try to get in touch with Klecka?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to get in touch with Klecka because I didn't know what to do with those tractors whose owners wanted to go to the villages of the plain. One of these tractors were the ones that I had stopped, and I wanted to learn from Klecke as to what to do with the civilian population that wanted to go to those villages. I was in a very difficult situation because of the tendency of some civilians to go to those villages and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, could you please turn to page 88 of the Albanian transcript. It's page 73 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could switch to the Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "O.L.: On 25th and 26th of July there was a big offensive on Lapusnik and Serb forces actually took over this place and the whole place was empty and some prisoners were released at -- on this day. Isn't it correct that you ran into a large group of released prisoners in Kroimire that were brought there on a tractor? "S.B.: Yes. Yes, I've seen them. "O.L.: And can you describe this? "S.B.: Yes, as far as I can remember it was this -- it was these moments when the civilian population was moving, was fleeing. So it was a total chaos, mess. Frankly -- frankly speaking, when I -- when I came across this -- this tractor, I thought that they were civilians -- yeah, I thought they were civilians -- civilian population and I wondered why all males on this tractor. So I stopped the tractor and I asked, Where are you coming from? And they say -- they said, We come from Lapusnik. They explicitly said, We are coming from the prison of Lapusnik. And I was taken a bit aback at this time so I didn't know how to react to this. I told them to wait. So I told them to -- I told them to wait and I made it clear to them that I was going to get -- to gather information on what to do further with them. I'll -- I've tried to get -- to get and speak on the phone. Fortunately there were people from Klecka there at the time -- "O.L.: In Kroimire? "S.B.: Yeah, in Kroimire. People from Lapusnik, people leaving Klecka but coming from Lapusnik. And then there was -- there were rumours that these detainees were released. I don't know how long it did last for me to -- to gather information about this. But what I know is that I returned to them and I said to them, You're free to go. And then I just made a point. And as you understand, it's an offensive going on and if you take the Lipjan direction you practically -- you practically will run into the Serb hands. So that's all I could say -- offer to them as a sort of information, because as I told you it was a total mess at that time. But what I knew for certain is that if they would go from this place to the Serbian hands that they would be killed for sure. Yeah, well they might be -- I might be missing details because it's a vague memory because of the circumstances at that time of -- this is more or less all about this meeting with them. Later on I inquired about this. Yeah, later I inquired simply because I was worried of probably having made any mistakes or -- no, they just -- they just said to me -- they calmed me down, No, you've acted in the right way. You've treated -- well, I -- I was rather worried about that because everybody was running away from me at that time.
